accuracy.evidence: Checked against Development Matters (DfE 2023): 3 and 4 year olds 'explore how things work' and 'explore and talk about different forces they can feel'; NGSS K-PS2-1 and K-PS2-2 (compare effects of pushes on motion; design to change speed or direction). Physics: released from rest, a car starting higher reaches the bottom faster (v = sqrt(2gh) ignoring losses) and, with a roughly constant rolling resistance on the floor, its stopping distance grows in proportion to the drop height, which is exactly how the lab spaces the flags (one unit per book). Flat-faced objects stay unless the slope passes the friction angle, so the text says 'stay put, or slide if the slope is very steep'.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the beliefs young children show in ramp play: that heavy things roll and light things do not (heavy tag, m4 light ball vs heavy brick), that anything round rolls whatever way it sits (the tin can prediction and the round tag), that a gentler, longer slope is faster (race step, gentle and same tags), and that to reach further you change the target rather than the slope (teddy tag). The fair-test idea (change only the books) is in m8 and the adult notes.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagramp is the only lab with a book-stacked board whose top is dragged up a book at a time, a shared run model that accelerates down the board then decelerates on the floor with flags left at each stopping point, a tube that must be tipped from its flat end onto its curved side before it rolls, and a two-lane slope race. The pushes-and-pulls lab varies push strength on flat ground; here the push is gravity and only the slope changes. Shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Step 1 makes the height-distance link visible as a row of numbered flags (1, 2, 4, 3 books); step 2 splits five toys into rolls or stays by shape; step 3 shows that roundness alone is not enough, the curved side must touch the slope; step 4 repeats the height rule as a race the child predicts; step 5 asks the child to use the rule to stop the car by the teddy, with 'add a book' or 'take a book off' feedback when it misses.

predictions.evidence: Three locked-in guesses: whether more books make the car slower or faster (some children think a steeper ramp 'stops' the car at the bottom), whether a brick rolls like a ball (tempting yes because both are 'toys on a slide'), and whether a round tin can standing on its flat end rolls (tempting yes because it is round). Each is then tested directly by letting go, and the reveal names the child's pick.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions, each wrong option tagged: gentle (gentle slope is slow), same (the race showed a difference), flat (flat sides stay put), round (round but standing on its flat end), up (things never roll uphill by themselves), less (less steep stops sooner), teddy (change the slope, not the target), heavy (weight does not decide) and colour (shape decides). Every message names the slip and restates the rule in a sentence a 4 year old can follow.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses words like slope, round, flat, steeper and roll in sentences of 3 to 12 words; the lab prompts are short commands ('Drag a toy to the top of the slope.'). Adult text names the curriculum statements and explains the physics without equations in the body. validate_lessons readability limits pass for both learner and adult text.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid paragraph gives one testable fact (a board on books is a slope; round rolls, flat stays; the can's flat end; more books go further). Adult paragraphs give the curriculum links, the science, the common mistakes with a fair-test warning, and what each lab step does. The filler gate passed and the explanation is under the 12% overlap limit with every other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark: the books stack, board, car, flags and teddy fit at 390 px with the floor running to the right edge; the toy shelf of five boxes fits in one row; race lanes keep their 'Top ramp' and 'Bottom ramp' labels clear of the cars; young-mode buttons are 56 px tall.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a button twin (Add a book, Take a book off, Let it go, one button per toy, Let go and Lay it on its side, Top car and Bottom car); the canvas aria-label is updated with every result ('2 books: the car went a bit further.'); walk.cjs found zero axe WCAG 2.1 AA violations in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13, and every task completes with Show me.
